The house resumed from Monday, May 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. 97, respecting the Waterton Glacier International Peace Park-Mr. Murphy-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 1-Proclamation.

Mr. Chairman, the
committee will remember that last evening I was in search of information with respect to this park, and I was able to obtain some from the remarks of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy). In justice to the bill and in justice to myself I do not think there is anything which would justify my opposition, in fact I think I will be obliged to support the bill but I regret very much the circumstances under which it was brought into existence. Why was it necessary to convert two previous national parks into an international peace park at a time when the Turtle mountain peace garden was just developing through the initiative of the people themselves? If ever a movement started spontaneously and with the real spirit of peace behind it, it was the Turtle mountain peace garden. When men put their hands in their pockets and get behind a proposition of this kind, it shows they have faith in the proposition. It is a comparatively easy matter for a body of Rotarians to shout for a park on the boundary line between the two countries when it does not necessitate their paying out any money. They appeal to the respective governments to go to it, they say they are behind it and forget the effect it may have on other proposals. There seems to be a desire on the part of larger bodies represented by the Waterton Glacier International Peace Park to thrust themselves into the front, at this time regardless of the effect it may have on other similar enterprises. The government will have to change its attitude unless it wants to be considered guilty of pre-natal strangulation of the Turtle mountain peace garden. That is what it is, particularly when it is realized that the

International Peace Park
birth date is due in less than two months July 14. The government should attempt to retrieve itself from occupying that unenviable position. Why is it necessary to move at this time? Are either of these parks, Waterton or Glacier in Alberta and Montana respectively, going to run away in the meantime? They have been there from time immemorial and they will be there after we have all passed away. The government should have waited at least until the birth date of the Turtle mountain proposition instead of butting in at this critical time.
It would seem as though this government cannot do the smallest public service without putting its foot in it. It disregards entirely the biblical injunction to "let not their good be evil spoken of." This park in Alberta is a good thing but no one can contemplate it without feeling that it has been conceived in a wrong spirit, one quite contrary to the spirit of peace. It seems to me a most astonishing thing that no matter what this government does it seems to go at it in the wrong way. That may be due to some innate cussedness on our part over here, but-
Hear, hear.

-I can refer to a dozen instances like this, although this is the most recent outstanding ease of acting in haste and repenting at leisure. If ever a body of men went at a thing wrong end foremost, it has been hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with this park. I should like to read to the committee a telegram which shows how some of our Dakota friends feel about this matter. This telegram was sent by the representatives of the Protective Peace Garden Association of North Dakota to Hon. Gerald P. Nye, of the United States Senate.
It reads:
The United States section of the International Peace Garden Protective Association comprising the towns of Saint John, Rugby, Dunseith, Bottineau, Souris, including all religious, fraternal and social service organizations of the entire Turtle mountain area in mass indignation meeting assembled, vigorously protest against the prior passage in the United States Senate of the Glacier-Waterton Peace Park bill being as it is a parasite originating in and subsisting upon the very life blood of the international peace garden Turtle mountain project from whose prior inception and organization the former has purloined its crest, motto, synonym and ideal and thus masked is invading an international field sacred in the arts of the Bchool children and the men and women of both countries. It is a heart-thrust that must be averted. Surely Senator Walsh, an executive committee member of the peace garden project, will see the deception being practised, denounce it and withdraw the measure.
If the government could see its way clear to adopt that course without defaulting in its international agreement with the United States, that is what it should do in justice to itself and to the Turtle mountain proposal. If the government believes in having only one park between the Rocks' mountains and Winnipeg, then it must continue with the one represented by this bill and pay no regard to the proposition at Turtle mountain. If it believes in two parks, why should not both parks be treated alike? In view of the international obligations which apparently have been entered into with respect to this Alberta foothill park, that is the only course which can be followed in fairness to the province of Manitoba and that part of Saskatchewan which * was behind Manitoba. Turtle mountain should be made a national park and treated the same as the other one-Watertown glacier. Will the Minister of the Interior say that he will be good enough to take this matter under his, as we call it, very serious consideration? If it does not do that, then I am afraid he must be prepared to face trouble in Manitoba in the future. He will be preparing nails for his own political coffin. I have no such designs against the minister because for some reason or other I rather respect him. He is rather the opposite to some of the rest of us, he is a patient and mild mannered man. I know he would not tramp on a fly or a spider, and because of that I know I shall not receive the same kind of offensive reply as my right hon. leader did from the Prime Minister when he offered certain suggestions a few moments ago. In my opinion the only solution of this problem is to convert Turtle mountain peace garden into a national park, provided of course that the members of that organization of which I am a member-the international peace garden committee-are agreeable. Turtle mountain is being put in a relatively subordinate position to the park at the foothills of the Rockies, and nothing but disaster can result to the former unless some such proposal as I have suggested is taken up. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance naturally do not want to entertain any proposal that will involve further financial outlay at this time. Let them at least make the statement that possibly that might be the best solution and they will be pleased to enter into negotiations with respresentatives of the Turtle mountain peace garden with that end in view. I do not care a continental what the government does with the suggestion. That is the best proposal I can think of, and unless it or
International Peace Park

something better is followed, some hon. members from Manitoba are liable to be badly hurt as a result of the government's blundering action in this respect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The ex-Minister of Agriculture is unduly concerned about this situation. The matter was first brought to my attention by a suggestion that the congress of the United States desired to name the park which is contiguous to the Waterton park in Alberta, a peace park, and as regards the use of the word "peace" between countries that are contiguous, it seems to me no harm can be done if the word is used many times. What I said to the Minister of the Interior was substantially what was read last evening by the ex-Minister of Agriculture from a letter of the Under-Secretary of State, namely, that if the United States congress enacted the legislation in question and gave to the park on the United States side of the forty-ninth parallel of latitude the name "Waterton Glacier International Peace park," we would be prepared to do so with respect to that portion of this area that comprises the Canadian park, now known as the Waterton park. But I made it clear that this action would not be taken until after such action had been taken by the United States and the bill had been signed by the president.
In order to show the good faith of parliament, the Minister of the Interior placed the bill upon the order paper and it stood there, not for any reasons such as the suspicions of the hon. gentleman suggested last evening, but until the president had signed the bill passed by the United States congress. That bill was signed, I think, some ten days ago. After it had passed the Senate and the House of Representatives, it stood for some time unsigned. When the Minister of the Interior was advised that the bill had been signed by the president, he proceeded, when the opportunity offered, with the introduction of his bill, and I am sorry that the hon. gentleman last evening suggested that the minister made no explanation, for he did make a concise and clear explanation of the reasons for taking the action. The bill now stands for further consideration by the house.
Waterton Glacier park is some 700 or 800 miles west of the suggested peace garden. It seems rather strange to suggest that an open park, through which runs the boundary line between two countries, which is to be maintained on the Canadian side as a park as heretofore and on the United States side as a park as heretofore, but bearing the name "International Peace park," and which is between 700 and 800 miles west of the peace

garden, should be inimical or destructive to the value of that peace garden. For my part I cannot follow that reasoning. I cannot understand in the least how it can be said to interfere with the peace garden in any way, shape or form. One is a natural park, just as nature has left it, except that roads have been constructed, hotels erected and various means taken to render its natural beauties more available to those who visit it. That is the Waterton park; that is the Glacier park. Now that they are merely to be known as one international peace park for the purpose of indicating that a boundary line passes through the park and divides two great countries and two great peoples who have lived in peace for many years and who, we all hope, will continue ever to live in terms of amity, good-will and peace, how that can affect a peace garden between Dakota and Manitoba, I am unable to understand. The very fact that the Minister of Agriculture in this government and the ex-Minister of Agriculture, are both, I believe, members of the executive or directing body of the peace garden organization; that the peace garden park, if you call it a park, because it is a garden, is very near the constituency of the Minister of the Interior in the province of Manitoba and that this peace park is west of the peace garden not only by part of Manitoba but the whole of Saskatchewan and is well towards the mountains in Alberta, should, it seems to me, in itself indicate that the government is not endeavouring, to "use the language which the hon. gentleman used last night, to play any favourites with regard to those organizations. In the one instance a name is given to an international park and the word that has been introduced is "peace" -international peace park-toy the action of the congress of the United States and the parliament of Canada. In the other case a voluntary organization, much to be commended, has established a peace garden some 800 miles east of that, between the state of Dakota and the province of Manitoba. That is the position.
I have recited the circumstances under which this bill finds a place upon the order paper and the exact reasons for its introduction, and certainly so far as I am able to understand from any persons with whom I have talked and who know the circumstances, they find it a little difficult to realize why you should imperil the existence of the one by giving a name to the other.

I like the recital which the Prime Minister has given. If it had been given last night, it would have been news to me, but now that we have the in-

International Peace Park
formation from the Minister Of the Interior and others, there is nothing new in his recital. Still, I thank him for it. Apparently the Prime Minister is unable to enter into the conception of the Turtle mountain proposition. It originated four years ago with the spirit of peace within it, and the people who were interested in it were prepared to put their money behind it, the same in Dakota as in Manitoba. Just as this first proposition is on the point of being born-July 14- another project, international in nature, national at the present time, but proposed to be made international, has sprung into existence. It would be, if you like, a very commendable enterprise at any other time later than this; but not having by any means been born necessarily of a peace conception it is going to assert itself regardless of all consequences to the smaller enterprise at the Turtle mountain. I may be a fatalist or something of that nature, but I believe no great good can come of anything that is born of hate, jealousy, strife, or of any improper motive, and before this government can hope for any great results from any proposal they choose to designate a peace proposition, it should be originated with peace motives behind it. Whatever the present motive may be, there is no doubt what will happen to the Turtle mountain proposition unless it is sponsored by something stronger than private enterprise at a time like the present. Even supposing we had sufficient capital to take care of it at the outset how are you going to maintain it from month to month and from year to year when it has to live largely on private givings and under the shadow of such a great enterprise 'as the one proposed by (his bill? Last night I used the expression "park at the foothills," as if on a parity with the Turtle mountain project, but I must admit I did not know then the extent of its present development. I have not one word to say against the proposition referred to in the bill, but it is coming into existence at a crucial time when it simply means the death of the other proposition. I speak of what I know fiom experience in such matters, and I speak of what the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches must know. To finance privately a proposition of this kind now is one thing, but it was a vastly easier thing four years ago. Then it was thought nothing of to undertake a great proposition like that at Turtle mountain, but to do it now is an utter impossibility as I see it, and that is why I am urging the government to back up a little and start over again, and do for Turtle mountain what they are proposing to do in this bill for Waterton-Glacier peace park. Then you will
really start on a peace basis with some chance of promoting peace, but as I indicated last night I do not see much object to be gained by precipitating disappointments and friction between the Canadian provinces for the sake of promoting peace between parts of Canada and parts of the United States. I am sorry if the Prime Minister cannot see that point of view. I can understand him refraining from entertaining any proposition which means more expenditure at this time. I do not know that my proposition would involve immediate expenditure. I do not even know if it would meet with the approval of the Turtle Mountain Peace Garden committee.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: They have never applied for governmental action. .

I know they have not, and that is all the more reason why they have my entire sympathy. I have been in undertakings, not so huge as that but of the same nature, where the undertaking depended upon the voluntary offerings of individuals and I know what has happened to some of them, and how some of them hit me. I know just about what the finish of this Turtle mountain peace garden will be unless the government metes out the same kind of financial treatment in the one case as in the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Might I assure the hon. gentleman that no commitments as to expenditures on this park as a peace park have been given or asked for-not any; and nothing has been added to the expenditures that ordinarily are made in Waterton park, nor has it been requested. It is merely the question of a name because the two parks are contiguous and are known as the Glacier park on the one side and the Waterton park on the other.

I am aware of that but a large expenditure has already been incurred and further expenditures will no doubt be incurred, for some development must take place in order to indicate and emphasize the international aspect of the park after this ' bill goes through.

I would like to commend the government for their action in making Water-ton park part of an international peace park. If I could I would gladly say something to allay the fears of the hon. member for Melville. I do not suppose I could do that except by assuring him that here are two parks lying opposite each other on the two sides of the international boundary, on the one side Glacier park, and on the other side Waterton park. Waterton lake itself, which is the
International Peace Park

reason for that district being preserved as a national park, lies in the centre of Waterton park and extends into Glacier park, with about half of it in each park. It is an ideal site for an international peace park. There are some seven or eight hundred miles between this new international peace park and the peace garden, and I would suggest to the hon. member for Melville that when he goes west this summer he come out to Alberta and we will take him down to Waterton and show him this new international peace park. I am sure that if he could only see the location and the surroundings he would withdraw all opposition to this bill. He might still press for some assistance for the peace garden, but that is an entirely different matter. I do not think that the formation of the park asked for in this bill should be held up in any way because the hon. member for Melville may think that some assistance should be given to the peace garden. The two do not conflict at all, and I think it was a very happy suggestion to make these two parks an international peace park.

Did my hon. friend hear the telegram that I read a few moments ago, sent to a United States senator by the people of Turtle mountain on the Dakota side? They feel about the same way as I do. I am not holding up this bill, and I have no thought of doing so. I would vote for it at once if it came to a vote. I think it is an excellent idea, but why should not similar treatment be meted out to Turtle mountain when nothing less will suffice to bring it into existence and maintain it under the new conditions occasioned by this bill. That is my view, and if my hon. friend will come down to Saskatchewan or on a visit to Turtle mountain I shall be very glad to accord him all the courtesies, but I am afraid that unless the government supports the proposition I shall not have that pleasure.

Just one word in regard
, to this project and I promise not to detain the committee or defeat the passage of my own bill. When the committee rose last night I was saying that along our international boundary we have many monuments and memorials to the peace that has existed between this country and the United States for one hundred years. One such memorial is located on the boundary line between British Columbia and the state of Washington, at White Rock, British Columbia, and at Blaine in the state of Washington. We have also the international peace bridge between Bridgeburg, Ontario, and Buffalo, New York, and we hope 
that this summer will see brought into being these two other memorials, namely, the international peace garden located on the boundary between Manitoba and North Dakota and the Waterton Glacier international peace park on the boundary line between the province of Alberta and the state of Montana. I do not share the fears of the hon. member for Melville that simply by naming this area as an international peace park we are in any way jeopardizing the success of the peace garden idea. I do not share those fears for this reason:	The peace garden idea was brought
into being through the voluntary efforts of citizens who are interested in promoting peace between the two countries, and in inculcating in the minds of the young the idea of peace for which all right-thinking people are striving. I do not see how, simply by naming an area some eight hundred miles to the westward as an international peace park, we are in any way jeopardizing the peace garden project. I agree with the Prime Minister that this does not interfere with the other project at all. It does not interfere in the slightest with the sentiment that has brought the peace garden idea into being. When we have people so much interested in bringing home to the minds of the young the ideal of peace, surely they are not going to cease their efforts now when their ideal has so nearly reached its consummation.

This reference to the supreme court, as I have already said, was primarily for the purpose of securing from the court an opinion as to the rights of the dominion as against the provinces in so far as the waters and water powers are concerned. In order that the principles set out in this factum may be thoroughly undSrstood it would be well for me to say at this point that in my judgment the St. Lawrence river is not merely an interpro-vineial river, but an international river. As the river flows through more than one province, it is an interprovincial river. It is an international river also because of the fact that we have certain treaties with the United States in regard to it, and one of the most important points in one of those treaties to which I desire to call the attention of the house is this: Article XXVI of the treaty of Washington of 1871 reads in part as follows:
The navigation of the river St. Lawrence, ascending and descending from the 45th parallel of north latitude, where it ceases to form the boundary between the two countries, from, to. and into the sea, shall forever remain free and open for the purposes of commerce to the citizens of the United States, subject to any laws and regulations of Great Britain or of the Dominion of Canada, not inconsistent with such privilege of free navigation.
It will be seen by that, Mr. Speaker, that the citizens of the United States have the right of free navigation on this river. That right arises by treaty between Great Britain and the United States. Therefore, when I make the statement that in my judgment this river is not only interprovincial but international in character, that is the ground for my statement. Furthermore, there is the treaty of Washington of 1909. By that treaty, an international board of commissioners was set up. When it comes to a question of navigation on the St. Lawrence river, any possibility of impediment, any question of free ascent or descent of that river by the citizens of the United States or Canada, must be submitted for decision, under the treaty of 1E09, to the international joint board. Therefore on that ground also we have in the St. Lawrence not only an interprovincial but an international river.

As example, one might mention the Trent canal in Ontario, or the! old Beauharnois canal in Quebec. There is another point of view I should like to bring to the attention of the house which arises out of the action of this parliament last year in declaring the new canal to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. By that title the dominion will become owners of the canal. By virtue of the legislation passed last year declaring this work to be to the general advantage of Canada I cannot for the life of me see how any argument can be lodged against the contention that the dominion owns the waters flowing through that canal. And Bourinot says further:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.
In my opinion this resolution if passed would be a direct order from the house to the government to do certain things which would involve an expenditure of public money. Therefore, I say such a resolution is not in order when moved by a private member.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is to be regretted that the resolution was not framed in the language which would permit Your Honour to rule it in order. However, I can imagine no question of recent years which has so stirred up public indignation and given rise to such scandal as this whole question of Beauharnois. "I believe that there is no government in Canada to-day that does not regret that it has parted with some of those natural resources for a consideration wholly inadequate and on terms which do not reflect the principle under which the crown holds natural resources in trust for all the people." That eloquent declaration of this basic principle is in the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) uttered not long ago. I submit to Your Honour and to the house that this whole project, conceived in greed and bom in political corruption, is now about to die of illegality. I propose to show, in the first place, that the act of the province of Quebec incorporating the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, and the amendments thereto, are completely outside the powers of the legislative assembly of that province and that therefore the acts themselves and everything permitted thereunder have no legal foundation, and any securities issued, works done or constructed under the authority of those acts are without legal backing. I submit further that the dominion parliament alone has the right to pass the necessary legislation to empower such works and undertakings as are involved in this development. I take as my authority the British North America Act, and I refer hon. members to section 92, which sets forth the powers of the provincial legislature. Subsection 10 of section 92 reads as follows:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:-
(a) Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the pi'ovinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province.
Clause " c " of this subsection reads as follows:
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
What is my authority for the statement that such works as these are outside the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec? I draw the attention of the house to a definition of that particular section of the British North America Act given in Clement's Canadian constitution, third edition, 1916, page 731. The paragraph is headed Companies' "Objects," and reads:
The purposes or objects to be served by incorporation are, like the possible subjects of legislation, numberless; but it may not be quite useless to consider some possible objects which touch closely the class-enumerations of the British North America Act. The "works and undertakings," for example, mentioned in section 92, No. 10, have been described by the privy council as physical things. Such of them as extend, actually or potentially, beyond the limits of a province are within the exclusive control of the parliament of Canada: and are manifestly not provincial objects for the establishment. control, and operation of which a provincial company could be incorporated. And the same remark applies to such undertakings as, though entirely located in one province, have been declared to be for the general advantage of Canada.
The act passed last year by this house put the whole development of this canal and all works and appurtenances thereto outside the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec. The principle declared in Clement's stamps it as an object other than provincial. Clement is clear and his opinion has been cited in privy council cases. I submit that this government should take into careful consideration the result of the legislative action in connection with this question. We should be careful in examining this matter to distinguish between works and undertakings and services. Businesses may be conducted for the purpose of service. The T. Eaton Company may be incorporated by a province and send its catalogues and ship its goods to other provinces. That does not constitute it an interprovincial company, nor does it place it outside the powers of a province to incorporate. But where a company is incorporated with powers to extend its own lines its own material
Does not the same question apply to the Ontario hydro?

I would not be at all surprised if it did. In regard to the power and canal works on the St. Lawrence river, I am absolutely convinced that as they are interprovincial, nay more, international in character, they are not within the competence of either Quebec or Ontario. There is no doubt in my mind on that point and I am glad the hon. member raised it.
A further fact in connection with this case is this: it was referred to by the hon. member for Acadia this afternoon. This canal is not an isolated canal. It is not a canal in the sense that some canal, say, down in the mari-times would be, or possibly a canal out in the province of Alberta. This canal is already declared to be a link in the great waterways project, the deep seaway. Have I authority for that? May I submit to the house that the original incorporation of this company under section 11 of chapter 72 of the statutes to which I have referred stated that the company shall be empowered to construct a canal not exceeding 150 feet English measure
Beauharnois Power Project

in width. Such a canal might have been regarded as so unimportant as possibly to be within the competence of the province of Quebec, but subsequent amendments, as in section 6 of the act of 1910, entirely changed this and gave the company power to widen the canal to 300 feet or to build a new canal 1,100 feet in width. It is getting bigger all the time, you see. Finally the act of 1930 gave the company power to construct a canal of the magnificent capacity of approximately 4,000 feet in width, capable of taking the entire flow of the St. Lawrence. This clearly indicates to me, and I hope to hon. members of this house, that the scope of the work was not a mere provincial canal or an irrigation ditch or anything of that kind, but a work to fit in with and be a part of the great deep seaway of the St. Lawrence. This view is upheld by many authorities. Almost every engineer who has been called upon to advise upon the matter has declared that it is such a link in the deep seaway and must be so regarded. Engineer Holgate, Engineer Acres, the report of Mr. St. Laurent to the minister of that day, have so held. But I do not have to go back to the opinions of these men. This government has decided it, and the previous government has decided it. I quote from the words of the right hon. leader of the government as reported at page 2113 of Hansard of April 18, 1932. He said:
We have indicated, as I said at the very threshold of my observations, that as the project was by common consent, alike by the late administration and by this, treated as an undertaking that was a link in the St. Lawrence waterway and that the canal should be a canal that would be available to navigation if as and when that undertaking is proceeded with-
A link, mark you. Again on the same page he says:
But having regard to the relation of this enterprise to navigation and to its being a unit in the development of the St. Lawrence waterway,-
And so forth.

I have no
objection to my hon. friend stating that the present government have designated it as a link in the canal system, but he is under a misapprehension in asserting that that was definitely stated by the previous government. If my hon. friend will look at the agreement he will see that I am correct.

If there is any hon. member in this house who has any doubt as to the intentions of the company or as to the knowedge on the part of those who were interested in granting the lease as

to the intentions of the company, then I shall be glad to hear an explanation from my hon. friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart). No public man of intelligence who studies this thing will be deceived in that matter. There is no question that the late administration did know that the Beauharnois Power Company did actually offer to the late government this canal free of charge to be a part of the deep seaway, and hon. members know it was so and it was accepted as such.

I do not
wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but they did not definitely state it was to be accepted as such although constructed for the purpose.

I will leave my hon. friend to explain it. The Beauharnois . Company itself had no delusions in the matter, for in many of its prospectuses it stated definitely that the canal would be a link in the deep seaway. I have here, for example, the best known of these prospectuses, entitled Physical Facts and Financial Figures. They are well worth reading, especially the financial figures. They are very illuminating. Some time in the future, politicians and historians will look back upon this whole affair as one just as fantastical as any fairy tale that came out of the Arabian Nights. At page 6 of this prospectus the company says:
In providing deep water navigation in its power canal the Beauharnois Power Corporation is providing one of the major links in the deep waterways by canalizing all the wholly Canadian section of the river, save for the stretch around the Lachine rapids at Montreal.
It must be clear already to hon. members who have been studying this question, and most of them I presume have been, more or less, that an undertaking such as this, anything that is so interconnecting, provincially speaking, as this, anything that is so international as this, obviously is not within the power of the province of Quebec to decide upon, nor can it be within the power of the province of Quebec or for that matter the province of Ontario, to legislate in respect to such matters. If further support of my argument in this regard is required I would refer hon. members to the factum presented, as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) stated this afternoon, on behalf of the late administration to the Supreme Court of Canada. At page 106 of the factum, paragraph 135, we find the following:
Linder section 91. No. 29, and section 92, No. 10 (a), of the British North America Act, actual or constructive extension beyond the limits of a province is a necessary feature of the work or undertaking in order to confer

Beauharnois Power Project
legislative jurisdiction upon the dominion parliament concerning same or to incorporate companies with objects in relation thereto, but as to the latter, it is now well established that it is the potential scope of the authorized objects and not the area of their actual exercise or operation which determines the character of the work or undertaking as being federal and where the authority conferred covers works or undertakings which may extend beyond the limits of a province, such works or undertakings are therefore non-local and fall to the exclusive jurisdiction of the dominion by virtue of section 92, No. 10 (a).
Then they cite certain cases. That was the position taken by the late administration and presented in the form of a factum by the Solicitor General for the Dominion of Canada before the Supreme Court of Canada. These legal gentlemen who made up the representatives of the government further stated at page 107, paragraph 137, of the factum:
The attorney general-
What attorney general? The Attorney General of the Dominion of Canada, the former attorney general:
The attorney general, therefore, submits that the parliament of Canada has legislative power under section 92, No. 10 (a) to authorize the Dominion government to construct and operate power works in interprovincial rivers provided the authority so conferred contemplates works which by themselves or their transmission lines physically extend beyond the limits of a single province or physically connect with works or lines in another province or which, though locally situate within a given province, form part of a general power undertaking authorized by the legislation and which includes, in fact or contemplation, similar works or lines or operation in one or more provinces and that for such purposes the Dominion parliament may confer power to purchase or expropriate provincial crown lands whether lying in the bed of an interprovincial river or otherwise.
There are clauses innumerable in the factum which bear out my contention that in the opinion of the late government, in the opinion of the attorney general and the group of lawyers who pleaded this factum before the supreme court, this parliament and this parliament alone had rights to legislate both in respect of power and canalization in connection with this project. By the way, the question of connection, the connecting work or undertakings comes in at this point. We see that in the act of incorporation the company has the potential right, or is supposed to have the potential right, to extend its works and undertakings into another province. But is there any evidence that it intends to use that right? All I have to do is to refer to the statement made to-day by the hon. member for Acadia that already the company has entered into contracts with the Hydro Electric Commission of the province
of Ontario for the sale of power to them. How can they supply power? The only way under heaven power can be got from the Beauharnois development to the province of Ontario is by wires, and those wires must connect. If they connect even within the province of Quebec with the Ontario power line they become interprovincial in character.
Mr. LaVERGNE: The contract is sufficient.

That is
quite true; the contract alone is sufficient to prove definitely the interprovincial character of this company. As I have already indicated, the fact that this is a link in a deep seaway canalization scheme also removes the project from the ambit of provincial legislation. A study of the map will reveal that this canal connects lake St. Francis with lake St. Louis. Lake St. Louis is a provincial lake, situate wholly within the province of Quebec. Lake St. Francis, however, is not only an interprovincial lake but it is international. A part of that lake is within the boundaries of the United States of America; a large part of it is within the province of Ontario. This canal, when completed must breach the dyke on the shore of lake St. Francis, and the minute it does that it becomes an interprovincial and international connecting link, a part of the connecting whole. It cannot be separated. When a project of this kind cannot be separated by itself within the limits of a province it ceases to be provincial in character, and becomes interprovincial.
Many authorities are at my disposal. I have not time to quote at length, but would refer hon. members to a case previously mentioned to-day. I refer to the argument of the late administration through the mouth of its attorney general. It is all there. But, more than that, the plans of the joint board of engineers show, as I have just indicated, that this project is interprovincial and international. To what extent? One third of lake St. Francis-that enormous amount, Mr. Speaker-one third of lake St. Francis is within the province of Ontario; almost the same amount is within the United States of America. Any movement of water from that lake via a canal such as the one proposed interferes with treaty obligations, and by virtue of that one fact becomes a matter within the sole jurisdiction of the dominion parliament.
I now come to the matter of treaty obligations, and the question whether or not they are important. I could cite case after case, report after report, dealing with this matter, but I have not time to do so. I shall refer
Beauhamois Power Project

only -to the remarks of the present chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals, Mr. McLachl'an. This gentleman gave evidence before the committee of this house which last year investigated the Beauharnois project. He was interrogated concerning difficulties involved in the project, and his evidence went to show that there was a certain current running crosswise at the entrance to the canal at lake St. Francis which would render exceedingly dangerous the navigation of ships at that point. In answer to the inquiry, "Is it a serious question?" he was referring to the matter of navigation and interference with treaty obligations, he answered, "Well, it is serious enough for me to feel that some change ought to be -made to mitigate conditions, otherwise I am sure we will have trouble both in using the waterway we have built under those conditions and in satisfying the American engineers when they come to approve of what we propose to do in Canadian territory." Then the question was asked, "And this change was never approved?" to which he replied, "This change was never approved." To my knowledge, so far as my information goes, the plans for this international work have not yet been approved. I submit that before work can be commenced, before navigation can ensue, there must be approval granted by the International Joint Commission under the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909.
There are other points to which I should like to draw the attention of hon. members. In summing up this phase of the matter, however, I suggest that the granting of authority, or the purporting to grant authority, to extend these works and undertakings as proposed in the -charter to which I have referred is not, I assert definitely-and I challenge legal correction, because after all I am only a layman, and am willing to listen to legal opinions in the matter-within the competence of the province of Quebec; the charter is ultra vires and illegal, and should be cancelled.
What about t-he interests involved? Serious -very serious. Not only should the charter be cancelled, but if the situation is left in its present position I hesitate to picture to the house what the possibilities may be. The federal government, however, can protect the public interest, and it is for that reason the amendment has been moved to-day. We have offered it humbly and respectfully, with no wish whatever to dictate, but simply to offer suggestions as to the manner in which the present federal administration should deal with the matter. In my opinion the federal government at this time can and should

reorganize the whole project. Both in respect to power output and canalization it should be declared a work in the national interest. There should be set up a federal hydro-electric commission to deal with the vast water power of this great international river.
On his oration in connection with this matter during the session of the year 1930 the Prime Minister, the leader of this government, asked the following question, "Do hon. members realize what this power development means? Do they realize that it means the future welfare and interests of not thousand or tens of thousands, but milions of people in the great yalley of the St. 'Lawrence?" I say the whole St. Lawrence project comes -within the scope of his statement. The whole St. Lawrence river scheme, involving as it does the development of 5,000,000 horse-power, 4,000,000 of which would belong to Canada, justifies and necessitates the creation of a federal hydro-electric commission to be operated in the public interest.
I opened my remarks to-day with a quotation from a speech by the leader of the government in which he said that governments regretted having given away for nothing, or next to nothing, valuable resources. Here is an opportunity for this government to save to the people of Canada one of the greatest and most powerful resources. They can declare this work to be in the national interest; they can create a federal hydro-electric commission. I submit if a part of the scheme can be developed in the national interest, the whole of it can be. The legality of the present situation should be decided. Let them take the matter to the privy council. I am satisfied as to what the decision will be.
The project cannot be left in its present state without grave dangers-yes, grave dangers-to the legitimate investments of Canadians and others. There is the further risk, worse than the one I have mentioned, that the great power interests may now seize upon the project, in its dying days, and grasp it to themselves, with the result that within a very short time this country would find itself under the absolute control of the Holt monopoly, the great Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company. There is no question in my mind as to the grave danger of that condition arising, if something is not done. In any case, Mr. Speaker, if this government does not act, if it merely leaves this company operating in the hands in which it now is operating, pouring into its coffers, as it has already been doing, millions of the taxpayers' money and on top of that proposing to make a loan to the tune of $15,000,000 or

Beauhamois Power Project
$16,000,000 more without deciding the question I have raised, why, the whole investment is liable to be lost. For it is certain that a valuable resource of this character is not going to be left in this questionable legal position. There will be, as I feel almost certain, case after case before the courts to determine the legality of it. There will be a definite fight-in fact I believe it commenced some time ago-it will continue, and other interests will combine and conspire to seize control of this project. If this government does not want to leave our investments in danger of being utterly lost it is time now for it to take over the whole project, and protect the rights of the people of Canada.
